doc.title: David Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 18, 2003

title: Economic realities and choosing projects
summary: Rewriting for octet for one gig, turning down a Porgy and Bess rewrite, and his quartet with Hamid Drake and Jaribu Shahid as a nucleus.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: How much of what you do when you decide on a project is driven by economic realities? Does that stop you?

Oh God. Oh yeah man. Because I’m always having to deal with that. Like for instance okay I come up with a wonderful concept I want to, I’ll say to my agent, I have this idea © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

about doing something with two choirs and a big band. Okay. Well how about like two singers and eight guys in the band? You know, I mean, well that’s knocked down. Every day. Like right now I was invited to Seattle to play at a concert with my Latin big band. And they only want to pay a fee, they’ll pay the transportation but not from Cuba. There’s problems with Cuba anyway. Okay I was going to get some Latin cats from New York. That’s even impossible. So now I have to re-write the music so that it actually is octet.

For that one gig. So now I’ve got arrange an album’s worth of music to play at this festival, and either truncate what I’ve done with the big band and make it smaller — I mean you can’t use the same music, it’s going to sound like crap you know. Any arranger knows that. You just have to do it over again. Otherwise it’s not going to sound — so that’s work. That’s serious work. To me that’s two weeks of work right there, just for this one gig. And to this booker, they just say well it’s a gig. I say yeah, but you know, you’ve got to get me more for that. That’s like the Nice Jazz Festival, they wanted to give me some money to do, they wanted me to re-write “Porgy & Bess.” And it was like the money was sizeable, I mean it was like $25,000. And I looked at my schedule and finally I said no. Because for me to change — I mean that would like change my life for the next six months, for me to re-write “Porgy & Bess.”

For one gig, man. I couldn’t do it. I had to say no, I can’t. Because I mean I’m not going to just — if I’m going to do it, I’m going to do it. I’m not going to do it half ass. Because then I’d have a bad reputation for that. So that’s the first time I said no. No, I can’t do it. You’ve got to get the next guy.
The nature of the business seems to be that everybody’s got multiple projects. I can imagine how hard it must be to get the people you want for either recording, or to do those concerts.

Yeah. Well you know what I’ve done is I have a nucleus and my nucleus is my quartet. Hamid Drake and Jaribu Shahid, as a trio. I mean those two guys are pretty much my nucleus in everything that I’m doing right now. So when the rhythm section is strong, you seem like you could build anything around it. It’s like you’ve got your motor and you’ve got your steering wheel and you’ve got — all you needs is some seats and a chassis. And then the ornaments and horns and brake lights you can put around it.
